prompt: What does persistent storage mean?
choices: Data that is copied into a variable at the start of a program
Data that only one program is allowed to read
Data that is saved to disk and survives after the program stops running
Data that Python keeps in memory for the whole run of the program
explain: Variables vanish when a program ends. Writing to a file makes the data persist on disk.

prompt: What is in log.txt after this program runs?
code:
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("one\n")
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("two\n")
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("three\n")
choices: Only the line three
The lines one, two and three
The lines one and three
Nothing, because the file was opened three times
explain: The last open uses "w", which empties the file before writing, so only three survives.

prompt: What does opening a file in "a" mode do?
choices: It opens the file for reading only and fails if the file is missing
It empties the file and then lets you write to it
It opens the file for reading and writing at the same time
It adds new data to the end of the file and keeps what was already there
explain: Append mode writes at the end of the existing content, and it creates the file if it does not exist yet.

prompt: A file named d.txt holds the three lines a, b and c. What does this print?
code:
with open("d.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
print(lines)
choices:
'a
b
c
'
['abc']
explain: readlines returns a list of strings and each one keeps the newline character that ended the line.

prompt: The file d2.txt holds some text. What does this print?
code:
with open("d2.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()
    rest = f.read()
print(repr(rest))
choices: The whole file again
None
It raises a ValueError because the file was already read
explain: The first read moves the position to the end of the file, so a second read finds nothing and returns an empty string.

prompt: The file d3.txt holds the lines first and second. What does this print?
code:
with open("d3.txt", "r") as f:
    a = f.readline()
    b = f.readline()
print(repr(a), repr(b))
choices: 'first' 'second'
'first\nsecond\n' ''
'first' ''
'first\n' 'second\n'
explain: readline returns one line at a time and includes the newline character at the end of each.

prompt: Why does a program need to close a file it has written to?
choices: To make sure the buffered data is actually written to disk and the resource is released
Because Python refuses to open any other file while one is still open
Because a file that is left open loses the data it already held
To convert the file from binary format back to text format
explain: Writes can sit in a buffer until the file is closed, and closing also frees the system resources the file was using.

prompt: What does this program print?
code:
with open("c.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("x")
print(f.closed)
choices: False
True
None
It raises a NameError because f only exists inside the with block
explain: Leaving the with block closes the file automatically, and the variable f is still in scope afterwards.

prompt: The file missing.txt does not exist. What happens?
code:
with open("missing.txt", "r") as f:
    print(f.read())
choices: It creates an empty missing.txt and prints an empty line
It prints None
It raises a PermissionError
It raises a FileNotFoundError
explain: Read mode never creates a file, so opening a file that is not there raises FileNotFoundError.

prompt: Which file modes will create the file when it does not already exist?
choices: Only "a"
Only "r"
Both "w" and "a"
None of the writing modes, the file must be created by hand first
explain: Write mode and append mode both create the file when it is missing, while read mode raises FileNotFoundError.

prompt: What is in wl.txt after this program runs?
code:
lines = ["a", "b", "c"]
with open("wl.txt", "w") as f:
    f.writelines(lines)
choices: Three lines reading a, b and c
One line reading abc
One line reading a b c
Nothing, because writelines needs a newline in each string to work
explain: writelines does not add newline characters, so the three strings run together on one line.

prompt: The file it.txt holds the lines 10, 20 and 30. What does this print?
code:
total = 0
with open("it.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:
        total += int(line.strip())
print(total)
choices: It raises a ValueError because each line ends with a newline
explain: Iterating a file gives one line at a time, and strip removes the newline so int can convert the digits.

prompt: What happens when this program runs?
code:
with open("num.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write(42)
choices: It writes 42 to the file
It writes the text "42" to the file
It writes nothing and leaves the file empty
It raises a TypeError because write only accepts strings
explain: write takes a string, so a number has to be converted first, for example with str(42) or an f-string.

prompt: What is the main advantage of the with statement over calling open and close by hand?
choices: It makes reading the file faster
It lets you open a file that does not exist in read mode
The file is closed automatically even if an error happens inside the block
It removes the need to pass a file mode to open
explain: The with statement closes the file when the block ends, including when an exception is raised part way through.

prompt: What does this program print?
code:
with open("w.txt", "w") as f:
    n = f.write("hello")
print(n)
choices: hello
True
None
explain: write returns the number of characters it wrote, and "hello" is five characters long.

prompt: What is the difference between a syntax error and an exception?
choices: A syntax error can be caught with try and except, an exception cannot
A syntax error stops the program from running at all, while an exception happens while the program is running
A syntax error only happens in files, an exception only happens with numbers
There is no difference, the two names mean the same thing
explain: Python refuses to run code with a syntax error, but an exception is raised during execution and can be handled.

prompt: What does this program print, in order?
choices: try only
finally runs only
try, then finally runs
finally runs, then try
explain: The finally block runs before the function actually hands its return value back, so its print appears first.

prompt: What does this program print, in order?
choices: bad, then done
ok 12 only
ok 12, then done
bad, then ok 12, then done
explain: No exception is raised, so the else block runs, and finally always runs at the end.

prompt: What does this program print?
choices: specific
general
general, then specific
It raises a SyntaxError because ValueError comes after Exception
explain: Python checks except clauses top to bottom, and Exception matches first, so the ValueError clause is never reached.

prompt: When a try block has several except clauses, in what order should they be written?
choices: The most specific exception types first and the broadest ones last
The broadest exception types first so nothing escapes
Alphabetical order by exception name
The order does not matter, Python picks the closest match
explain: Clauses are tried in order, so a broad clause placed early would swallow the errors the specific clauses were meant to handle.

prompt: Which exception does this code raise?
code: age = int("twenty")
choices: TypeError
NameError
ValueError
SyntaxError
explain: int receives a string of the right type but the wrong value, which is exactly what ValueError reports.

prompt: Which exception does this code raise?
code:
person = {"name": "Ana"}
print(person["age"])
choices: IndexError
ValueError
AttributeError
KeyError
explain: Looking up a dictionary key that is not present raises KeyError.

prompt: When does Python raise an IndexError?
choices: When a variable is used before it is given a value
When a list is asked for a position that does not exist
When two values of different types are added together
When a dictionary key cannot be found
explain: IndexError means the position asked for is outside the range of the sequence.

prompt: What does this program print?
choices: cannot divide by zero, then still running
bad value, then still running
cannot divide by zero only
The program crashes before printing anything
explain: The matching except clause handles the error, so the program keeps going and reaches the final print.

prompt: What does this program print?
choices: caught: ValueError
It crashes with an unhandled ZeroDivisionError
caught: cannot divide by zero
explain: The raise happens before any division, and printing the caught exception shows the message it was given.

prompt: What does the raise keyword do?
choices: It restarts the try block from the beginning
It reports the last exception that Python handled
It triggers an exception on purpose so the calling code knows something went wrong
It stops the program immediately without any error message
explain: raise is how your own code signals a problem, usually after a validation check fails.

prompt: What does this program print?
choices: caught: missing host
It crashes, because only ConfigError can catch a ConfigError
caught: ConfigError
caught: AppError
explain: A subclass of an exception is caught by a clause naming its parent, which is why exception hierarchies are useful.

prompt: Why would you define your own exception class instead of raising a built in one?
choices: Custom exceptions are the only kind that can carry a message
It names the problem precisely so calling code can catch just that kind of failure
Built in exceptions cannot be caught with try and except
Python runs custom exceptions faster than built in ones
explain: A named exception such as ConfigError makes the failure clear and lets callers handle it separately from unrelated errors.

prompt: What does this program print, in order?
choices: logging only
outer: gone only
logging, then outer: gone
outer: gone, then logging
explain: A bare raise inside an except block sends the same exception on to the caller after the local handling is done.

prompt: What does this program print?
choices: It crashes with a ValueError on the second item
explain: The bad item is skipped by the except clause, so only 3 and 5 are added.

prompt: Where in a traceback do you find the exception type and its message?
choices: On the last line, at the very bottom
On the first line, right after the word Traceback
In the middle, beside the file name
Tracebacks show only line numbers, never the exception type
explain: A traceback lists the call chain first and finishes with the exception type and message on the bottom line.

prompt: What does this program print?
code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("reports") / "summary.csv"
print(p.name, p.stem, p.suffix)
choices: summary.csv reports .csv
summary.csv summary .csv
summary summary.csv csv
reports summary .csv
explain: name is the file name with its extension, stem is the name without the extension, and suffix is the extension itself.

prompt: Why should you build a path with os.path.join or a pathlib Path instead of gluing strings together with a slash?
choices: Because gluing strings is slower for long paths
Because Python does not allow the plus operator on strings
Because the right separator is used on Windows as well as on Mac and Linux
Because only joined paths can be passed to open
explain: Windows uses a backslash while Mac and Linux use a forward slash, and the path tools pick the correct one for you.

prompt: On a Mac or Linux machine, what does this print?
code:
import os

print(os.path.join("data", "raw", "file.txt"))
choices: data raw file.txt
datarawfile.txt
['data', 'raw', 'file.txt']
data/raw/file.txt
explain: os.path.join inserts the separator the current system uses between each part.

prompt: What is a relative path?
choices: A path that always begins at the root of the file system
A path that is interpreted from the directory the program is running in
A path that points only to a folder and never to a file
A path that contains no file extension
explain: A relative path such as data.txt is resolved against the current working directory rather than the root of the disk.

prompt: The file report.txt does not exist. What does this print?
code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("report.txt")
print(p.exists(), p.suffix)
choices: False .txt
True .txt
False txt
It raises a FileNotFoundError
explain: A Path object is just a name, so exists reports False while suffix still reads the extension from the text.

prompt: The file notes.txt does not exist yet. What happens?
code:
with open("notes.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("hi\n")
choices: It raises a FileNotFoundError
It raises a PermissionError
It does nothing, because append needs an existing file
It creates notes.txt containing the line hi
explain: Append mode creates the file when it is missing, then writes at the end.

prompt: What does this program print?
code:
line = "  Hello World \n"
print(repr(line.strip()))
choices: '  Hello World '
'HelloWorld'
'Hello World'
'  Hello World \n'
explain: strip removes whitespace, including the newline, from both ends but leaves the space in the middle alone.

prompt: What is the difference between read() and readlines()?
choices: read returns the whole file as one string, readlines returns a list with one string per line
read returns a list of lines, readlines returns one string
read works only on small files, readlines works only on large files
read closes the file afterwards, readlines leaves it open
explain: Both load the whole file, but read gives a single string while readlines splits it into a list.

prompt: The file input.txt holds the single line hello. What is in output.txt afterwards?
code:
with open("input.txt", "r") as source:
    with open("output.txt", "w") as target:
        for line in source:
            target.write(line.upper())
choices: hello
HELLO
Nothing, because a file cannot be read and written in the same block
HELLO written twice
explain: Nested with statements let you read one file and write another, and upper converts each line before it is written.

prompt: What is a context manager?
choices: A function that reads a whole file into memory at once
A module that keeps track of which files a program has opened
A special kind of exception used for file errors
An object that sets a resource up when a with block starts and cleans it up when the block ends
explain: File objects are context managers, which is why the with statement can open a file and reliably close it again.

prompt: What happens when this program runs?
code:
with open("bad.txt", "w") as f:
    print(f.read())
choices: It prints an empty line
It prints the previous contents of bad.txt
It raises an error because the file was not opened for reading
It raises a FileNotFoundError
explain: A file opened in "w" mode is write only, so calling read on it is an unsupported operation.

prompt: The file data.txt does not exist. What does this program print?
choices: no such file only
no such file, then None
None only
It crashes with an unhandled FileNotFoundError
explain: The handler prints its message and returns None, which the caller then prints.

prompt: In except ValueError as e, what does the name e refer to?
choices: The exception object, which carries the error message
The line number where the error happened
The name of the function that raised the error
A copy of the value that failed to convert
explain: The as clause binds the exception object, so printing e shows the message it was created with.

prompt: What is in events.log after this program runs?
code:
def log(message):
    with open("events.log", "a") as f:
        f.write(message + "\n")

log("start")
log("stop")
choices: Only the line stop
Only the line start
The line start followed by the line stop
One line reading startstop
explain: Append mode adds to the end each time, and the newline in the write keeps the entries on separate lines.

prompt: Why is a bare except: that catches everything discouraged?
choices: It runs more slowly than a named except clause
Python plans to remove it from the language
It can only be used once per program
It hides bugs by swallowing errors you never expected or planned for
explain: Catching everything makes real programming mistakes look like handled conditions, which makes debugging much harder.

prompt: What does this program print?
choices: 7seven
It crashes with a ValueError
explain: The first call converts successfully and the second falls back to 0, so the sum is 7.

prompt: Which list contains only text files?
choices: notes.txt, data.csv, config.json
photo.jpg, notes.txt, song.mp3
archive.zip, program.exe, image.png
report.pdf, data.csv, video.mp4
explain: Text files hold human readable characters, while images, audio, archives and executables are binary.

prompt: What is true about this program?
code:
with open("a.txt", "r") as source, open("b.txt", "w") as target:
    target.write(source.read())
choices: Only a.txt is closed at the end of the block
Only b.txt is closed at the end of the block
It raises a SyntaxError because with cannot take two files
Both files are closed when the block ends
explain: A single with statement can manage several resources, and every one of them is closed when the block finishes.

prompt: A program must read a file whose name the user types in. Which approach matches the practices taught in this unit?
choices: Read the file with no checks and let the program crash if it is missing
Wrap every file operation in a bare except: that prints nothing
Check the path with Path.exists, then open it inside a with statement and catch FileNotFoundError and PermissionError
Copy the file to a fixed name first so the program can always open the same path
explain: Validate first, use with so the file is always closed, and catch the specific errors that this operation can realistically raise.
